title: Natural, made and tested: choosing materials like a scientist
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 2 Chemistry: Unit 3.1 'Natural and made materials', Unit 3.2 'Properties of materials', Unit 3.3 'Using the right material' and Unit 3.4 'Testing materials'. No textbook needed.
summary: Glass is made from sand, and a cotton kurta began as a fluffy plant. Your child sorts materials into natural ones and ones people make, and follows how cotton becomes cloth, sand becomes glass and clay becomes brick. They learn the property words rigid, flexible, absorbent, waterproof and transparent, sort with a Venn diagram, and run fair tests with a ruler, coins, a table and a block graph. They hear the true story of a cloudy liquid that became one of the strongest fibres ever made, and they bury materials in soil to see which ones break down.
builds_on: Class 1: object and material, the property words hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy, stretchy, see-through and waterproof, simple tests, and where materials come from. Next: Changing materials (Class 2) heats, cools and burns them. Class 3 adds transparent, translucent and opaque, magnetic metals and branching keys.
subconcepts: raw materials and how people change them
a material's journey: cotton to cloth, sand to glass, clay to brick, oil to plastic
property words: rigid, flexible, waterproof, absorbent, transparent, strong
a material's properties decide its uses
a fair test: change one thing, keep the rest the same, measure
recording results in a table and a block graph
the cost of a material to the Earth
texture and sound: how a material feels and how it carries or absorbs sound
goals: By the end your child can sort materials into natural and made, and explain that made materials are changed from natural ones.
By the end your child can tell the journey of three materials from raw material to object.
By the end your child can use the words rigid, flexible, absorbent, waterproof and transparent correctly.
By the end your child can plan and carry out a fair test, saying what they changed, what they kept the same and what they measured.
By the end your child can record results in a table and a block graph and say what the results show.
By the end your child can explain what biodegradable means and why it matters which materials we choose.
words: a material found in nature: wood, wool, cotton, stone, clay
a material people make by changing natural ones: glass, plastic, steel, paper, brick
the natural material a made material starts from, like sand for glass
stiff: it keeps its shape and does not bend
it soaks up water, like a sponge or towel
it does not let water through
you can see clearly through it
a test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same
a chart of blocks or bars that shows numbers so you can compare them
two overlapping circles for sorting things that can belong to both groups
it can be broken down by tiny living things, such as bacteria and fungi, into soil, water and gases

days.title: Natural or made?
days.goal: Recall last year's materials and split them into natural and made.

steps.title: Remember the crow?
steps.do: Ask: 'Last year a crow built a nest of wire, twigs, coir, cotton and wool. What is the difference between an object and a material?' (the object is the thing, the material is what it is made of). 'Why did the crow use wire on the outside?' (strong and bendy). Then hand your child a steel spoon and a wooden spoon: 'Same object, two materials. Which one would you stir hot dal with, and why?' (wood, because steel gets hot).

steps.title: Natural or made hunt
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Go round the house, and the balcony or compound if you can. Your child finds 6 natural materials (a stone, a leaf from a potted plant, a twig, wool, a shell, soil or clay) and 6 made materials (a plastic bucket, a glass bottle, a steel plate, a paper bag, a floor tile, a nylon rope). Put them in two heaps on a mat. Ask about each one: 'Did a person change this from something else?'

steps.title: The tricky ones
steps.do: Hold up a cotton kurta. Ask: 'Natural or made?' Let your child argue. The answer: cotton is a natural material, but the cloth was made by people who spun and wove it. Then a wooden chair (natural wood, shaped by people), paper (made, from wood), a floor tile (made, from baked clay). Say: 'Every made material started as a natural one. People changed it.' Write the rule on a card for the wall.

need: a steel spoon and a wooden spoon

days.title: A material's journey
days.goal: Follow raw materials as people change them, and start the burial test.

steps.title: Journey chains
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Your child draws four journey chains with arrows, one box per step, while you tell each one. Cotton: cotton plant → fluffy bolls picked → spun into thread → woven into cloth → kurta. Sand: sand from a river or beach → melted in a furnace hotter than any kitchen fire → blown or moulded → glass bottle. Clay: clay dug from the ground → mixed with water and shaped → dried and baked in a kiln → brick. Oil: oil pumped from deep underground → changed in a factory into tiny beads → melted and moulded → plastic bucket. Ask: 'Which journey needs the most fire?'

steps.title: The steel the world wanted
steps.do: Tell voice v1: about 2,000 years ago, ironworkers in South India and Sri Lanka heated iron with plant material in small sealed clay pots. They made a very good steel, called wootz. Traders carried it across the sea, and smiths in the Middle East made it into famous swords with wavy patterns. Ask the voice's question.

steps.title: Start the burial test
steps.do: Set up Experiment e3. Bury, in a pot of damp soil (from a potted plant or a nursery bag), small labelled pieces of: a banana peel, a cotton rag, a piece of newspaper, a plastic bag, a piece of foil and a leaf. Push a lolly stick next to each. Ask your child to predict which will be gone in two weeks. Write the predictions down and keep the soil damp.

need: a pot of soil from a plant pot or a nursery bag
banana peel, cotton rag, newspaper, plastic bag, foil, a leaf

days.title: The scientist's property words
days.goal: Learn the exact words for properties, and hear the true story of a cloudy liquid.

steps.title: Property stations
steps.do: Set up five stations on a table, each with three things and a label. RIGID or FLEXIBLE: a steel ruler, a plastic ruler, a sheet of paper. ABSORBENT or not: a sponge, a steel plate, a cotton cloth (drip water on each). WATERPROOF or not: a plastic bag, newspaper, foil. TRANSPARENT or not: a clear bottle, a cardboard box, butter paper. STRONG or WEAK: a jute string, a cotton thread, a strand of hair (pull gently). Your child visits each station, tests, and says a sentence with the new word: 'The sponge is absorbent.'

steps.title: Story: The Cloudy Liquid
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain. Ask: 'Why did people think the liquid was no good?' (it was cloudy and runny, not clear and thick like the good ones). 'How did Stephanie find out what it could do?' (she tested it: it was spun into a thread and pulled). Then tell voice v2 and ask its question.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1. Read each item aloud. In the written questions, push for a reason: 'because…'

need: a dropper or spoon and water

days.title: The climbing water test
days.goal: Run a fair test with measuring, a table and a block graph.

steps.title: What makes a test fair?
steps.do: Ask: 'If I race you, but I start halfway down the road, is it fair?' (no). 'In a science test, what must be the same?' Explain: we change ONE thing (the material) and keep everything else the same (the size of the strip, the water, the time). Then we MEASURE what happens. Ask: 'Can we answer "which is the prettiest towel?" with a test?' (no, people disagree). 'What about "which material soaks up water fastest?"' (yes, we can measure it).

steps.title: Which material soaks up water fastest?
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Cut strips 2 cm wide and 15 cm long of five materials. Hang them side by side so each dips 1 cm into coloured water at the same moment. After 5 minutes, your child measures with a ruler how high the colour has climbed up each strip, and you write it in a table: material, centimetres climbed.

steps.title: Make a block graph
steps.do: On squared paper, your child colours one square for each centimetre the water climbed, one column per material. Ask: 'Which column is tallest? Which material is most absorbent? Which would you choose for a towel, and which for a raincoat?' (the most absorbent for the towel, the one the water did not climb for the raincoat).

need: strips 2 cm wide and 15 cm long of kitchen towel, newspaper, printer paper, cotton cloth and a plastic bag
a pencil or stick, 5 clothes pegs or tape, and two piles of books
a tray or wide bowl of water with a few drops of food colour or ink
a ruler, a timer, squared paper and crayons

days.title: The strongest paper
days.goal: Test strength fairly and learn that one result is not enough.

steps.title: Which paper is strongest?
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Cut strips 2 cm wide and 15 cm long from toilet paper, a paper napkin and a kitchen towel. Hang one strip from the table edge under a heavy book, with a small plastic bag hooked on the bottom. Your child adds one-rupee coins one at a time, gently, until the strip tears. Count the coins. Test two strips of each paper. Ask: 'Why did we cut every strip the same size?'

steps.title: Why test twice?
steps.do: If the two tries gave different numbers, ask: 'Why might that be?' (a strip had a tiny tear, a coin was dropped hard). Say: 'Scientists repeat tests so one accident doesn't fool them.' Ask: 'What else could change how strong a strip is, besides the paper?' (how wide it is, a small cut at the edge, folding it double).

steps.title: Check the burial test
steps.do: Gently dig up the banana peel in Experiment e3 with a spoon and look: has it changed colour? Is it soft? Push it back, re-bury and water the soil a little. Don't dig up the others yet.

need: strips of toilet paper, a paper napkin and a kitchen towel
a heavy book, a paper clip bent into a hook, tape and a small plastic bag
about 80 one-rupee coins of the same design (or a cup of dry rice and a tablespoon)

prep.task: Collect about 80 one-rupee coins of the same design, or keep a cup of dry rice and a tablespoon

days.title: Sorting and choosing
days.goal: Sort with a Venn diagram and match materials to jobs.

steps.title: Floor Venn diagram
steps.do: Lay two hoops or two dupattas in overlapping circles on the floor. Label one FLEXIBLE and one WATERPROOF. Your child places 10 objects: a plastic bag (both, in the middle), a steel plate (waterproof but not flexible), a cotton hanky (flexible, not waterproof), a rubber glove (both), a wooden block (neither, outside both circles), a sheet of paper, a foil sheet, a glass bottle, a woollen sock, a balloon. Ask: 'What does it mean to be in the middle? What about outside both circles?'

steps.title: Design challenges
steps.do: Ask your child to choose materials for: a raincoat for a pet dog (waterproof, flexible, light), a window for a submarine (transparent, very strong, waterproof), a mop (absorbent, flexible), a bridge for ants across a bucket (rigid, light, strong). For each, they must name the properties first, then the material. There are several good answers.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 together. For the Venn question, let your child draw the two circles first.

days.title: Materials on stage
days.goal: Use drama, art and listening to feel properties from the inside.

steps.title: The great audition
steps.do: Do Activity a4. You are the director of a film called 'The Umbrella'. Your child plays, one at a time, Paper, Plastic, Wool and Steel, trying out for the job of umbrella. Each one boasts about a property and admits a weakness. Paper: 'I'm light and cheap!' (but I go soggy). Plastic: 'I'm waterproof and flexible!' (but I last for hundreds of years if thrown away). Wool: 'I'm warm and soft!' (but I soak up rain). Steel: 'I'm strong!' (but too heavy and rigid to fold). You, the director, ask each one a hard question. Then your child chooses who gets the job and gives the reason. Now the job is 'towel', and the winner changes. Ask: 'Is any material good or bad, or only good or bad for a job?'

steps.title: Texture rubbings
steps.do: Your child lays thin paper over surfaces around the house and rubs the side of a peeled crayon over them: a jute mat, a coin, a leaf, a tile, a wooden table, a cane chair, a brick wall, a steel grater. Each rubbing gets a label: material, natural or made, rough or smooth. Ask: 'Could you tell what the material is from its rubbing alone?' Mix the rubbings up and test each other. Say: 'Texture is how a surface feels: rough, smooth or bumpy. Scientists look at textures much more closely with microscopes.'

steps.title: Listen through the table
steps.do: Your child puts one ear flat on a wooden table and covers the other ear with a hand. You tap the far end of the table gently with a fingernail. Then your child lifts their head and listens to the same tap through the air. Ask: 'Which was louder?' (through the table). Now lay a folded blanket on the table, put the ear on the blanket and tap again. Ask: 'What changed?' (the tap is much quieter). Say: 'Sound travels well through hard materials like wood and steel. Soft, fluffy materials absorb sound. That's why recording studios have soft walls.' Try the side of a steel almirah too.

need: paper hats or dupattas for costumes (optional)
a wooden table, a folded blanket, a steel almirah if you have one

days.title: What breaks down in soil?
days.goal: Dig up the burial test and think about materials that do not break down.

steps.title: Dig it up
steps.do: Dig up everything in Experiment e3 on a newspaper. Compare with the predictions. Your child sorts the pieces: CHANGED A LOT (banana peel, leaf), CHANGED A LITTLE (newspaper, cotton), NOT CHANGED (plastic, foil). If you have waited only a week, the newspaper and cotton may not have changed yet. Say the word biodegradable: it can be broken down by tiny living things, such as bacteria and fungi, into soil, water and gases. Ask: 'Which made materials broke down? Which did not?'

steps.title: The compost question
steps.do: Tell voice v3. Some plastics now say 'compostable' on the packet. Ask: 'How could we test if a packet that says compostable really is?' (bury it like our test, and check after weeks or months). 'Who should test it: the company or someone else? Why?'

steps.title: Material Journey board game
steps.do: Play the board game g1. Each player is a material on a journey from the Earth and back again. Read each square aloud and say whether it helps or slows the material.

need: the printed board, a die and counters

days.title: The bag project, and teach it back
days.goal: Use a fair test to choose the best vegetable bag, and explain everything.

steps.title: Project: the best vegetable bag
steps.do: Do the project. Your child tests three cloth or paper bags for carrying vegetables home: strength (how many potatoes before it tears or stretches badly), waterproof (one spoon of water), and whether it can be washed and reused. They fill in a small table and choose a winner, with reasons.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3. The last questions have no single answer. Ask your child to give reasons and to say how they would test their idea.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child explains to a family member: natural and made materials (with a journey), the five property words, how to make a test fair, what the burial test showed, and the cloudy-liquid story. Then ask the check questions.

need: 3 bags: a cloth bag, a paper bag, a jute or plastic bag

sections.p: Sort these materials.

A sponge soaks up water. It is…
A steel ruler does not bend. It is…
You can see clearly through a window because glass is ____.
A raincoat keeps water out because it is ____.
A kurta is made of cotton. Is it natural or made? Explain your answer.
Why would a towel made of plastic be a bad towel?
Kavya tests which cloth soaks up water fastest. Which must she keep the same?
Which question can you answer with a test?
opts: Which towel soaks up water fastest?
Which towel does Paati like best?

sections.p: In a fair test we change only ____ thing.
Copy your climbing water results here.
Flexible, waterproof, both or neither?
Match the job to the best material.
In your paper test, one kitchen towel strip held 12 coins and the next held 20. What would you do, and why?
Design a raincoat for a pet dog. Which properties does it need? Which material would you pick?
In the burial test, which piece changed least?
Biodegradable means…
opts: it can be broken down by tiny living things
it is made in a factory

sections.p: Stephanie Kwolek, a chemist, made a liquid that looked cloudy. What did the test show?
opts: it made a very strong fibre

sections.p: Wootz was a famous ____ made in South India long ago.
Which break down in soil quickly, and which slowly or hardly at all?
Match the material to how it is made.
Stephanie Kwolek's liquid looked wrong, but it made a very strong thread. Can you always tell what a material can do by looking at it? How do you find out?
Plastic is waterproof, cheap and strong, and it lasts for a very long time. Is lasting a long time good or bad? When?
Invent a test to find out whether a 'compostable' cup really breaks down. What will you change, keep the same and look for?

experiments.title: The climbing water test: which material is most absorbent?
experiments.question: Which material soaks up water fastest, so the water climbs highest up it in 5 minutes?
need: strips 2 cm wide and 15 cm long of kitchen towel, newspaper, printer paper, cotton cloth and a plastic bag
a pencil or stick and 5 clothes pegs or tape
a tray or wide bowl with water about 2 cm deep, with a few drops of food colour or ink
steps: Draw a pencil line 1 cm from the bottom of each strip.
Peg or tape the strips along the stick so they hang down side by side.
Rest the stick on the two piles of books, over the empty tray. Add or remove a book until each strip's line is at the height of the water you will pour.
Lift the stick off. Pour the coloured water into the tray.
Put the stick back, so every strip dips in up to its line at the same moment. Start the timer.
After 5 minutes, measure how high the colour has climbed above the line on each strip, in centimetres.
Write each result in a table, then draw a block graph.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to put the five strips in order, from the one the water will climb highest to the one it will climb least, and to say why.
experiments.observe: The colour climbs highest up the kitchen towel, often 8 cm or more. It climbs less up the newspaper and the cotton, and only 2 or 3 cm up printer paper. It does not climb the plastic at all.
experiments.why: Absorbent materials are made of tiny fibres with narrow gaps between them. Water clings to the fibres and is pulled up the gaps. Kitchen towel is loose and fluffy, with many fine gaps. Printer paper is pressed flat, so it has fewer. Plastic has no gaps, so water cannot climb it. Keeping the strip size, the depth and the time the same makes the test fair, so the material is the only thing that changes.
experiments.safety: Wipe up spills so nobody slips. Food colour can stain, so use an old tray.

experiments.title: Which paper is strongest?
experiments.question: Which paper holds the most coins before it tears?
need: strips 2 cm wide and 15 cm long of toilet paper, a paper napkin and a kitchen towel, two of each
a paper clip bent into a hook, and tape
a small plastic bag with handles
about 80 one-rupee coins of the same design, or a cup of dry rice and a tablespoon
steps: Check each strip for tiny tears. Use only strips with none.
Lay the top 3 cm of a strip on the table and put the heavy book on it, so the strip hangs over the edge.
Fold the bottom 2 cm round the paper clip hook and tape it. Hang the bag on the hook.
Add coins one at a time, gently, counting out loud, until the strip tears. (With rice, add one level tablespoon at a time.)
Write down the number.
Test the second strip of the same paper, then the other papers.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which strip will hold the most coins? About how many?'
experiments.observe: Toilet paper strips tear first, often after about 15 coins. Paper napkin strips hold more, and kitchen towel strips hold the most, often about 60. Two strips of the same paper usually hold slightly different numbers.
experiments.why: Paper is a mat of tangled plant fibres. A thicker paper, like kitchen towel, has more fibres across the strip to share the pull, so it holds more. A strip tears at its weakest spot, and every strip has a different weakest spot. That is why two strips of one paper give different numbers, and why we test more than once.
experiments.safety: Add coins gently and keep feet clear of the bag.

experiments.title: The burial test
experiments.question: Which materials can the soil break down?
need: a large pot or tub of damp soil, from a potted plant or a nursery bag
small pieces of banana peel, cotton rag, newspaper, plastic bag, foil and a leaf
steps: Bury each piece about 5 cm deep in a different part of the pot.
Mark each with a labelled lolly stick.
Keep the soil damp, not soaking, in a shady place.
On Day 5, check only the banana peel.
On Day 8, dig everything up and compare. If you can, wait until two weeks have passed since you buried them.
experiments.predict: Write your child's prediction for each piece: gone, changed, or the same.
experiments.observe: The banana peel and leaf turn brown, soft and broken. The newspaper and cotton go soft and may start to fall apart. The plastic and foil look almost the same.
experiments.why: Bacteria, fungi and small animals like worms feed on materials made from living things: peel, leaves, paper and cotton. These are biodegradable. Most plastics are made of long chains that these living things cannot easily break down, so they stay for a very long time and only break into smaller pieces. Foil is a metal and does not rot.
experiments.safety: Wash hands after handling soil. Use soil from a plant pot or a nursery, not from a drain or a dump.

activities.title: Natural or made hunt
steps: Find 6 natural materials and 6 made materials.
Put them in two heaps.
For each, ask: did a person change this from something else?
activities.outcome: Two heaps, and a first feeling for 'natural' and 'made'.

activities.title: Journey chains
steps: Draw a box for each step of a material's journey.
Join the boxes with arrows.
Do cotton, sand, clay and oil.
activities.outcome: Four journey chains for the wall.

activities.title: Floor Venn diagram
steps: Overlap two circles on the floor.
Label them FLEXIBLE and WATERPROOF.
Place each object: one circle, the middle, or outside.
activities.outcome: Your child understands that a thing can belong to two groups, one, or none.

activities.title: The great audition
steps: The grown-up is the director.
The child plays each material trying out for a job, boasting about a property and admitting a weakness.
The director asks a hard question.
The child chooses the winner and gives a reason.
Change the job and see if the winner changes.
activities.outcome: Your child sees that 'best' depends on the job, and can argue from properties.

project.title: The best vegetable bag
steps: Get three bags: a cloth bag, a paper bag, and a jute or plastic bag.
Decide what a good vegetable bag needs: strong, doesn't leak when vegetables are wet, can be reused.
Test strength: add potatoes one at a time and count how many before it tears or stretches badly.
Test whether it leaks: pour one spoon of water inside and look underneath.
Fill in a table and choose a winner, with reasons.
Talk about how many times each bag could be used again.
project.outcome: A small table of results and a reasoned choice of the best bag, which the family then uses.

game.title: Material Journey
rules: Each player chooses to be a material: cotton, sand, clay or wood.
Start at THE EARTH. Roll the die and move.
Read the square aloud. Do what it says.
The first to reach BACK TO THE EARTH wins, but you must explain one property of your material to finish.
squares: Dug or picked by hand: move on 1
Carried on a truck: roll again
A furnace: sand and clay go forward 2, the others go back 1
Tested: is it strong? Say a property
Thrown in a river: miss a turn
Broken down by bacteria and fungi: cotton and wood go forward 2

big: Every made material started as a natural one. So is anything really unnatural?
Is a material that lasts for ever a good thing or a problem?
Can you tell what something can do just by looking at it?
Who should test whether a company's product does what it says?
Should we choose the cheapest material, the strongest, or the kindest to the Earth?

challenge.q: People say paper bags are always better for the Earth than plastic bags. Is that true?
challenge.hint: It depends on how many times a bag is used. A 2011 study for England's Environment Agency found that making a paper bag harms the climate more than making a thin plastic one. So a paper bag must be used about 3 times to do better, and a cotton bag more than 100 times. But paper rots and thin plastic doesn't. Ask: what matters more, how a bag is made or where it ends up?

challenge.q: Some packets say 'biodegradable'. Does that mean they will vanish in your garden?
challenge.hint: Not always. Some only break down in very hot compost at a factory. A large study in Britain in 2022 found that many plastics labelled 'home compostable' had not fully broken down in people's home compost. Ask: what should a label have to prove?

challenge.q: Is glass a natural or a made material?
challenge.hint: People make glass by melting sand. But glass also forms in nature. Obsidian is a black glass made when lava from a volcano cools quickly, and lightning striking sand can make glass tubes. So the line between natural and made is not always sharp.

perspectives.view: Before a kurta reaches a shop, a farmer grew the cotton, often in great heat, and was paid only a small part of what the kurta costs. Ask: in the journey of a material, who gets the most money, and who does the most work?

Earthworms feed on dead leaves and peel in the soil. To a worm, a banana peel is food and a plastic bag is a wall they cannot get through. Ask: if worms could choose our materials, what would they choose?
Engineers test materials until they break, on purpose, so the real bridge never does. Ask: why is breaking things sometimes the most careful thing to do?

voices.who: The wootz steel makers of ancient South India and Sri Lanka
voices.idea: About 2,000 years ago, ironworkers in South India and Sri Lanka heated iron with plant material inside small sealed clay pots, called crucibles, to make a high-quality steel. It was traded across the Arabian Sea, and smiths in the Middle East made it into famous 'Damascus' blades with wavy patterns.
voices.then: Travellers and traders admired the steel. For a long time European smiths could not copy it.
voices.now: Archaeologists have found crucible steel sites in South India and Sri Lanka, and metallurgists have studied the blades and accept their Indian and Sri Lankan origin. The makers' names are lost, and the skill died out by the 1800s.
voices.ask: The makers of wootz wrote no books, but their steel travelled the world. How do we know what people knew, if they didn't write it down?

voices.who: Stephanie Kwolek (1923–2014) and Charles Smullen, DuPont, USA
voices.idea: In 1964 and 1965, Kwolek was looking for a light, strong fibre. She made a liquid that was cloudy and runny, when good ones were usually clear and thick. Instead of throwing it away, she asked Smullen, who ran the spinning machine, to spin it. The thread was, for its weight, far stronger than steel. It became Kevlar, used in protective vests, gloves and ropes.
voices.then: Smullen at first did not want to spin it, worried it would clog the machine. Once tested, the fibre amazed the company.
voices.now: Kwolek is honoured as a great inventor and was inducted into the US National Inventors Hall of Fame. Smullen's part is less often told.
voices.ask: What would have happened if Stephanie had judged the liquid by how it looked? Why was Charles's help needed too?

voices.who: Danielle Purkiss and colleagues, University College London, 'The Big Compost Experiment' (2022)
voices.idea: Thousands of people in Britain tested packaging labelled 'compostable' or 'home compostable' in their own compost heaps. Many of the items had not fully broken down when people checked.
voices.then: Packaging is labelled home compostable after tests in controlled conditions. Real home compost heaps are often cooler and less even than those tests.
voices.now: Scientists are still arguing about which labels are trustworthy and how they should be tested. Many agree that 'compostable' plastic needs the right conditions, which most homes don't have.
voices.ask: The company tested its packet, and ordinary people tested it too, and they got different answers. Whose test would you trust more, and why?

story.title: The Cloudy Liquid
text: I was born in a glass bottle on a hot afternoon in 1965, in a laboratory in Delaware, in America. My mother was a chemist called Stephanie Kwolek. That is how I think of her, anyway, though she would have laughed at being called the mother of a bottle of liquid.

Stephanie was looking for something that did not exist yet. Her company wanted a new fibre for car tyres: a thread lighter than steel wire, but just as strong, so cars could be lighter and use less fuel. For months she had been mixing long, chain-like molecules into liquids and sending them to be spun into threads. Most of the threads were weak. None was the one she wanted.

I was not what anyone expected. A good liquid for spinning, everybody knew, was clear and thick, like honey. I was thin and runny, like buttermilk. And I was cloudy. When Stephanie stirred me, I shimmered, grey and pearly.
Most chemists would have thrown me out. They would have thought tiny bits of dirt were floating in me, and started again.
Stephanie held me up to the window and looked at me for a long time. She did not throw me out.

Instead, she did something careful. She filtered me, pouring me slowly through a fine filter to catch any bits of dirt. If I were cloudy because of rubbish, the rubbish would stay in the filter and I would come out clear. I went through. Nothing was left behind. I came out just as cloudy as before.
So the cloudiness was not dirt. It was me. It was the way my long molecules had lined up together, side by side, like matchsticks in a box all pointing the same way.

The next step was the spinning machine. It pushed liquid through a metal plate full of tiny holes to make threads, like an idiyappam press pushing out strings of dough. It was run by a man called Charles Smullen. Stephanie carried me to him.
Charles looked at me and shook his head. 'I'm not putting that in my machine,' he said. 'It's cloudy. It's got particles in it. It'll block all the holes and I'll spend a week cleaning it.'
Stephanie told him about the filter. He still said no. She kept asking, politely and stubbornly. I sat in my bottle on her bench and waited.
At last Charles sighed and said, 'All right. Once.'

He poured me into the machine. I remember the squeeze of the tiny holes, and the strange feeling of becoming something new: not a liquid any more, but a thread, fine and golden-yellow, wound round and round a spool.

Then they tested me. They pulled me in a machine that measures how hard you must pull before a thread snaps. They pulled, and pulled, and I did not snap. They checked the machine to see if it was broken. It wasn't. They tested me again. For my weight, I was about five times stronger than steel. And I was stiff: I hardly stretched at all.

Stephanie and her colleagues kept working on me and my cousins, and the family of threads that grew from me became known as Kevlar. Today it is woven into vests that protect police officers and soldiers, into gloves that keep cooks' and glassworkers' fingers safe from sharp edges, into ropes that hold ships, and into the skins of spacecraft. Many people are alive because of it.

But I like to remember the bottle on the bench, and the window, and the cloudy light. Most people would have seen something wrong. Stephanie asked what I could do. And Charles, after first saying no, was willing to find out.
story.epiphany: You cannot know a material's properties by looking. You find out by testing. The cloudy, runny liquid broke everyone's rule, but when it was filtered (a test), and then spun and pulled (more tests), it proved to be one of the strongest fibres ever made. The turn is the pulling machine. Underneath: a woman scientist trusting her own careful checking, and a technician whose help made the discovery possible.
ask: Why did people think the liquid was spoiled?
What did Stephanie do to check whether the cloudiness was dirt? What did it show?
Why did Charles say no? Was he being silly or careful?
How did they find out how strong the thread was?
Have you ever judged something by how it looked and been wrong?

ideas.idea: Every 'made' material began as a natural one.
ideas.more: Glass is melted sand. Steel is made from iron, which comes from rock. Plastic is made from oil, and paper from mashed wood. People don't make materials from nothing. They change what the Earth gives.

ideas.idea: You find out what a material can do by testing it fairly, not by how it looks.
ideas.more: Change one thing, keep the rest the same, measure, repeat. The cloudy liquid looked useless and was one of the strongest fibres ever made.

ideas.idea: Tiny living things break down some materials quickly. Others last a very long time.
ideas.more: Bacteria and fungi break down peel, leaves, cotton and paper. Most plastics, glass and metals stay for a very long time. Choosing a material also chooses where it ends up.

unknowns: Nobody knows for sure how the old smiths of South India and Sri Lanka controlled every step of making wootz steel. Metallurgists have made similar steel, but whether they have matched it exactly is still argued about.
How long do the tiny broken bits of plastic stay in soil and sea, and what do they do to living things? Scientists are still measuring.
What new materials will chemists find next? Many good ones, like Kevlar, were surprises found by testing something that looked useless.

books.why: A materials scientist on steel, paper, plastic and more. The chapter on paper is good to read aloud before the bag test.

check.q: Name two natural and two made materials.
check.a: Natural: wood, wool, cotton, stone, clay. Made: glass, plastic, steel, paper, brick.

check.q: Tell the journey of glass or brick.
check.a: Glass: sand is melted in a very hot furnace and shaped. Brick: clay is dug, shaped, dried and baked in a kiln.

check.q: What does absorbent mean? Which material in our climbing water test was most absorbent?
check.a: It soaks up water. Usually the kitchen towel: the water climbed highest up it.

check.q: How did we make the climbing water test fair?
check.a: Every strip was the same size, dipped the same depth and timed for the same 5 minutes. Only the material changed.

check.q: Why do scientists repeat a test?
check.a: So one mistake or accident doesn't fool them. Results that agree are more reliable.

check.q: What happened to the plastic and the banana peel in the burial test? Why?
check.a: The peel rotted because tiny living things broke it down (it is biodegradable). The plastic hardly changed because they cannot easily break it down.

check.q: How did Stephanie Kwolek find out her cloudy liquid was special?
check.a: She tested it. She filtered it, then had it spun into a thread and pulled, and the thread was very strong.
